chapters.title: How I Began My Sea Adventure
paragraphs: There was no fresh attack from the mutineers — not so much as another shot from the woods. They had ‘got their rations for that day,' as the captain put it, and we had the place to ourselves and a quiet spell to tend the wounded and get dinner. The squire and I cooked outside, danger or no; and even out there we could hardly keep our minds on the work, for the horror of the loud groans that reached us from the doctor's patients.

Of the eight men who had fallen in the fight, only three still breathed — the pirate shot at the loophole, Hunter, and Captain Smollett; and of these the first two were as good as dead. The mutineer, indeed, died under the doctor's knife, and Hunter, for all we could do, never came back to his senses in this world. He lingered through the day, breathing heavily like the old buccaneer at home in his fit, but his ribs had been crushed by the blow and his skull cracked in the fall; and sometime in the night, without a sign or a sound, he went to his Maker.

As for the captain, his wounds were bad enough, but not dangerous. No vital organ had been struck. Anderson's ball — for it was Job who shot him first — had broken his shoulder-blade and grazed the lung, not seriously; the second had only torn and shifted some muscle in his calf. He would certainly recover, the doctor said; but in the meantime, and for weeks to come, he must not walk or move his arm, nor even speak if he could help it.
My own accidental cut across the knuckles was a flea-bite. Dr. Livesey patched it with plaster and tweaked my ears into the bargain.

After dinner the squire and the doctor sat a while by the captain's side in council; and when they had talked their fill — it being then a little past noon — the doctor took up his hat and pistols, buckled on a cutlass, slipped the chart into his pocket, and with a musket over his shoulder crossed the palisade on the north side and strode off briskly through the trees.

Gray and I sat together at the far end of the block house, to be out of earshot while our officers conferred; and Gray took the pipe from his mouth and clean forgot to put it back, so thunderstruck was he at the sight.
“Why, in the name of Davy Jones,” said he, “has Dr. Livesey gone mad?”
“Not he,” said I. “He's about the last of this crew I'd expect it of.”
“Well, shipmate,” said Gray, “mad he may not be — but if he isn't, then mark my words, I am.”
“My guess,” I replied, “is that the doctor has a notion of his own; and if I'm right, he's off now to see Ben Gunn.”

I was right, as it turned out; but in the meantime, the house being stifling hot and the little patch of sand inside the palisade blazing under the midday sun, another thought began to work in my head — one not nearly so sound. What I fell to was envying the doctor, walking in the cool shade of the woods with the birds about him and the sweet smell of the pines, while I sat grilling, my clothes glued to the hot resin, with so much blood around me and so many poor dead bodies lying about that I took a loathing of the place almost as strong as fear.

All the while I was swabbing out the block house and then washing up after dinner, this loathing and envy grew stronger and stronger, until at last, finding myself near a bread-bag with no one watching, I took the first step toward my escapade and stuffed both coat pockets with biscuit.

Call me a fool — and a fool I was, bent on a foolish, reckless act; but I meant to carry it out with every precaution I could. The biscuit, if anything went wrong, would at least keep me from starving well into the next day.
The next thing I laid hands on was a brace of pistols; and as I already had a powder-horn and bullets, I reckoned myself well armed.

The scheme in my head wasn't a bad one in itself. I meant to go down the sandy spit that divides the anchorage from the open sea on the east, find the white rock I'd marked the evening before, and see whether Ben Gunn had truly hidden his boat there — well worth doing, as I still believe. But certain I'd never be let out of the enclosure, my only plan was to take French leave and slip off when nobody was looking — and that bad way of going about it was just what made the thing itself wrong. But I was only a boy, and my mind was made up.

As it fell out, a fine chance came my way. The squire and Gray were busy helping the captain with his bandages; the coast was clear; I made a dash over the stockade into the thickest of the trees, and before anyone marked my absence I was beyond hail of my companions.
This was my second piece of folly, far worse than the first, since it left only two sound men to guard the house; but, like the first, it ended up helping to save us all.

I made straight for the east coast of the island, meaning to go down the seaward side of the spit and keep clear of any eyes at the anchorage. It was already late in the afternoon, though still warm and sunny. As I threaded the tall woods I could hear, far ahead, not only the steady thunder of the surf but a tossing of leaves and grinding of boughs that told me the sea breeze had got up stronger than usual. Soon cool draughts of air reached me, and a few steps more brought me out at the open edge of the grove, where the sea lay blue and sunlit to the horizon, the surf tumbling its foam along the beach.

I have never once seen the sea quiet around Treasure Island. The sun might blaze overhead, the air hang without a breath, the surface lie smooth and blue, and still these great rollers would be running all along the outer coast, thundering and thundering by day and by night; I scarcely believe there's a single spot on the island out of earshot of their noise.
I walked along beside the surf with great enjoyment until, judging I'd come far enough south, I took cover among some thick bushes and crept warily up to the ridge of the spit.

Behind me lay the sea, before me the anchorage. The sea breeze, as if it had blown itself out the sooner for its violence, had already died; in its place came light, shifting airs from the south and south-east, carrying great banks of fog. The anchorage, under the lee of Skeleton Island, lay as still and leaden as on the day we first entered it. The Hispaniola was mirrored there from truck to waterline, the Jolly Roger drooping from her peak.

Alongside lay one of the gigs, Silver in the stern-sheets — him I could always tell — while a couple of men leaned over the stern bulwarks, one in a red cap, the very rogue I'd seen astride the palisade some hours earlier. They seemed to be talking and laughing, though at that distance — over a mile — I could of course catch nothing of what passed. All at once a hideous, unearthly screaming broke out that gave me a bad start, until I recalled the voice of Captain Flint, and even fancied I could make out the bird by her bright plumage as she perched on her master's wrist.
Before long the jolly-boat pushed off and pulled for the beach, while the man in the red cap and his mate dropped below through the cabin companion.
About the same time the sun dropped behind the Spy-glass, and with the fog gathering fast it began to grow dark in earnest. I saw I had no time to lose if I meant to find the boat that evening.

The white rock, plain enough above the brush, stood still some eighth of a mile further down the spit, and it took me a good while to reach it, crawling, often on all fours, through the scrub. Night had all but come when I laid my hand on its rough side. Right below it lay a tiny hollow of green turf, screened by banks and a thick, knee-deep undergrowth that grew there in plenty; and in the middle of the dell, sure enough, stood a little tent of goat-skins, like the ones gipsies carry about in England.

I dropped into the hollow, lifted the flap of the tent, and there was Ben Gunn's boat — home-made if ever a thing was: a rough, lop-sided frame of tough wood with a goat-skin hide stretched over it, the hair turned inward. It was extremely small, even for me, and I can hardly think it would have floated under a full-grown man. There was a single thwart set as low as it would go, a sort of footrest in the bows, and a double paddle to drive her.

I had never then seen a coracle, of the kind the ancient Britons made; but I've seen one since, and I can give you no truer notion of Ben Gunn's boat than to say it was like the first and the worst coracle ever built by man. Yet it certainly had the coracle's great virtue, being very light and easy to carry.

Well, now that I'd found the boat, you'd think I had had enough of truancy for once; but by then another notion had taken hold of me, and I'd grown so stubbornly fond of it that I believe I'd have carried it out in the teeth of Captain Smollett himself. It was this: to slip out under cover of dark, cut the Hispaniola adrift, and let her run ashore wherever she chose. I'd quite convinced myself that the mutineers, after their repulse that morning, wanted nothing so much as to weigh anchor and put to sea; to stop that, I thought, would be a fine stroke, and now that I'd seen how they left their watchmen without a boat, it seemed it might be done at little risk.

Down I sat to wait for dark, and made a hearty meal of biscuit. It was a night in ten thousand for my purpose. The fog had now blotted out the whole sky. As the last of the daylight faded and went, utter blackness came down over Treasure Island. And when at last I shouldered the coracle and groped my stumbling way out of the hollow where I'd supped, just two points of light showed anywhere on the anchorage.

One was the great fire on shore, where the beaten pirates lay carousing in the swamp. The other, a mere smudge of light on the dark, marked where the ship lay at anchor. She had swung round to the ebb — her bow toward me now — and the only lights aboard were in the cabin; what I saw was just the glow of the strong rays from the stern window, thrown back off the fog.

The ebb had been running some time, and I had to wade through a long belt of swampy sand, sinking past my ankle more than once, before I reached the edge of the retreating water; then, wading a little way in, I managed with some strength and knack to set the coracle, keel down, on the surface.

chapters.title: The Ebb-tide Runs
paragraphs: The coracle — as I had every reason to learn before I was through with her — was a very safe boat for someone of my height and weight, buoyant and quick in a seaway; but she was the most contrary, lop-sided craft to handle. Do what you would, she made more leeway than anything afloat, and spinning round and round was the trick she did best. Even Ben Gunn himself owned that she was ‘queer to handle till you knew her ways.'

And know her ways I certainly did not. She turned every direction but the one I wanted; most of the time we went broadside on, and I'm quite sure I'd never have reached the ship at all but for the tide. By good luck, paddle as I might, the tide kept sweeping me down; and there lay the Hispaniola right in the fairway, hardly to be missed.

First she loomed up before me like a blot of something blacker than the dark; then her spars and hull took shape; and the next moment, it seemed (for the farther I went the brisker ran the ebb), I was alongside her hawser and had caught hold.

The hawser was as taut as a bowstring, so hard did the current drag her on her anchor. All round the hull, in the blackness, the rippling current bubbled and chattered like a little mountain stream. One cut of my sea-knife and the Hispaniola would go humming away down the tide.

So far so good — but then it came back to me that a taut hawser, cut all at once, is as dangerous as a kicking horse. Ten to one, if I were rash enough to part the Hispaniola from her anchor, the coracle and I would be flung clean out of the water.

That brought me up short, and had luck not once more stood my friend, I'd have had to give up the plan. But the light airs that had begun in the south-east and south had, after nightfall, hauled round into the south-west. Just as I sat pondering, a puff came, caught the Hispaniola, and pushed her up into the current; and to my great joy I felt the hawser go slack in my grip, and the hand I held it with dip a moment under water.

At that I made up my mind, took out my knife, opened it with my teeth, and cut one strand after another until the ship hung by only two. Then I lay still, waiting to part the last when a breath of wind should ease the strain once more.

All this while I'd been hearing loud voices from the cabin, but to tell the truth my mind had been so full of other things that I'd hardly listened. Now, with nothing else to do, I began to pay closer heed.

One voice I knew for the coxswain's — Israel Hands, who had been Flint's gunner in the old days. The other was my friend of the red night-cap. Both were plainly far gone in drink, and still at it, for even as I listened one of them, with a drunken shout, threw open the stern window and pitched something out — an empty bottle, I guessed. But they were more than tipsy: they were in a furious rage. Oaths flew like hail, and now and again came such an outburst that I felt sure it must end in blows. But each time the quarrel blew over and the voices grumbled lower for a spell, until the next flare-up came, and passed in its turn without result.

On shore I could see the glow of the great camp-fire burning warm through the trees along the beach. Someone was singing a dull, old, droning sailor's song with a dip and a quaver at the close of every verse, and seemingly no end to it but the singer's patience. I'd heard it more than once on the voyage, and these words came back to me:
“But one man of her crew alive, What put to sea with seventy-five.”

And I thought it a ditty rather too gloomily fitting for a company that had taken such cruel losses that very morning. But, from what I saw, all these buccaneers were as callous as the sea they sailed.
At last the breeze came; the schooner edged sidewise and loomed nearer in the dark; once more I felt the hawser ease, and with one good hard saw I parted the last fibres.

The breeze had little hold on the coracle, and almost at once I was swept up against the bows of the Hispaniola. At the same time the schooner began to turn on her heel, swinging slowly, end for end, across the current.

I worked like a fiend, for I looked every moment to be swamped; and finding I couldn't push the coracle straight off, I now shoved dead astern. At last I cleared my dangerous neighbour; and just as I gave the final shove, my hands fell on a light cord trailing overboard across the stern bulwarks. I grabbed it on the instant.
Why I did so I can hardly tell. At first it was mere instinct; but once I had it fast in my hands, curiosity got the better of me, and I made up my mind to have one look in at the cabin window.

I hauled in hand over hand on the cord, and when I judged myself near enough, raised myself — at huge risk — to about half my height, and so got a view of the cabin roof and a slice of what lay within.

By now the schooner and her little consort were slipping along quite fast through the water; indeed we had already drawn level with the camp-fire. The ship was ‘talking,' as sailors say — loudly — treading the countless ripples with a ceaseless weltering splash; and until I got my eye over the sill I couldn't make out why the watchmen had raised no alarm. One glance settled it — and one glance was all I dared take from that unsteady skiff. It showed me Hands and his companion locked in a deadly wrestle, each with a hand at the other's throat.

I dropped back onto the thwart, and none too soon, for I was near overboard. For a moment I could see nothing but those two furious, blood-red faces swaying together under the smoky lamp, and I shut my eyes to let them grow used to the dark again.
The endless ballad had come to its end at last, and the whole thinned company round the camp-fire had broken into the chorus I'd heard so often:
“Fifteen men on the dead man's chest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

I was just thinking how busy drink and the devil were at that very moment in the cabin of the Hispaniola, when I was startled by a sudden lurch of the coracle. At the same instant she yawed sharply and seemed to change her course. Her speed, meanwhile, had strangely increased.

I opened my eyes at once. All round me were little ripples, combing over with a sharp, bristling sound and faintly phosphorescent. The Hispaniola herself, a few yards in whose wake I was still being whirled along, seemed to stagger in her course; I saw her spars toss a little against the black of the night, and as I looked longer I felt sure she too was wheeling to the southward.

I glanced over my shoulder, and my heart leaped against my ribs. There, right behind me, was the glow of the camp-fire. The current had turned at a right angle, sweeping the tall schooner and the little dancing coracle along with it; ever quickening, ever bubbling higher, ever muttering louder, it went spinning through the narrows toward the open sea.

All at once the schooner ahead gave a violent yaw, turning perhaps twenty degrees; and almost in the same breath one shout followed another from her deck. I heard feet pounding up the companion ladder, and knew that the two drunkards had at last broken off their quarrel and waked to their disaster.

I lay down flat in the bottom of that wretched skiff and devoutly commended my soul to its Maker. At the end of the straits, I felt sure, we must run into some bar of raging breakers, where my troubles would soon be over; and though I think I could have borne to die, I could not bear to watch my fate come on.

So I must have lain for hours, tossed endlessly to and fro on the swell, now and then drenched with flying spray, and never ceasing to expect death at the next plunge. Little by little weariness crept over me; a numbness, with now and then a stupor, settled on my mind even amid my terrors, until at last sleep came, and there in my sea-tossed coracle I lay and dreamed of home and the old Admiral Benbow.

chapters.title: The Cruise of the Coracle
paragraphs: It was broad day when I woke and found myself tossing off the south-west end of Treasure Island. The sun was up, but still hidden from me behind the great bulk of the Spy-glass, which on this side dropped almost to the sea in fearsome cliffs.

Haulbowline Head and Mizzenmast Hill were close at my elbow — the hill bare and dark, the head ringed with cliffs forty or fifty feet high and skirted with great heaps of fallen rock. I was barely a quarter-mile to seaward, and my first thought was to paddle in and land.

That notion was soon dropped. Among the fallen rocks the breakers spouted and bellowed; loud booming echoes, heavy sprays flung up and falling, followed one another second by second; and I saw myself, if I dared go nearer, dashed to death on the rough shore or wearing out my strength for nothing trying to scale the overhanging crags.

Nor was that the worst, for crawling together on the flat slabs of rock, or dropping into the sea with loud reports, I saw huge, slimy monsters — soft snails, as it were, of unbelievable size — two or three score together, setting the rocks ringing with their barking.

I've learned since that they were sea lions, and quite harmless. But the look of them, with the difficult shore and the high surf, was more than enough to put me off that landing-place. I felt readier to starve at sea than to face such perils.

Meanwhile I had, as I supposed, a better chance ahead of me. North of Haulbowline Head the land runs a long way out, leaving at low tide a broad stretch of yellow sand. North of that again comes another cape — Cape of the Woods, as the chart had it — thick with tall green pines that ran right down to the water's edge.

I remembered what Silver had said about the current that sets northward along the whole west coast of Treasure Island; and seeing from where I lay that I was already in its grip, I chose to leave Haulbowline Head behind and save my strength for a try at the kindlier-looking Cape of the Woods.
A great smooth swell ran on the sea. With the wind holding steady and soft out of the south, it had no quarrel with the current, and the billows rose and fell without breaking.

Had it been otherwise, I must have perished long before; but as it was, it was wonderful how easily and safely my little light boat could ride. Often, while I still lay in the bottom with no more than an eye above the gunwale, I'd see a big blue summit heave up close above me; yet the coracle would only bob a little, dance as if on springs, and sink down the far side into the trough as lightly as a bird.

After a little I began to grow over-bold and sat up to try my hand at paddling. But even a small shift in the weight makes a violent change in how a coracle behaves. I had hardly moved before the boat gave up her gentle dancing all at once, ran straight down a slope of water so steep it turned me giddy, and drove her nose, with a spout of spray, deep into the side of the next wave.

I was drenched and terrified, and fell straight back into my old place, whereupon the coracle seemed to recover her head and carried me as softly as before among the billows. Plainly she was not to be meddled with; and at that rate, since I could in no way steer her, what hope was left of my ever reaching land?

A horrible fear began to take me, but I kept my wits in spite of it. First, working with great care, I baled the coracle dry bit by bit with my sea-cap; then, raising my eye over the gunwale again, I gave my mind to studying how she contrived to slip so quietly through the rollers.

I found that each wave — instead of the big, smooth, glassy mountain it looks from shore or a ship's deck — was for all the world like a stretch of hills on dry land, full of peaks and flats and valleys. The coracle, left to herself, turning this way and that, threaded her way, so to speak, through the lower ground and shunned the steep slopes and high, toppling crests of the wave.

“Well, then,” thought I, “it's plain I must lie where I am and not upset the balance; but it's plain too that I can put the paddle over the side now and again, in the smooth places, and give her a shove or two toward land.” No sooner thought than done. There I lay on my elbows in the most trying posture, and every so often gave a feeble stroke or two to turn her head shoreward.

It was tiring, slow work, yet I plainly gained ground; and as we neared the Cape of the Woods, though I saw I must surely miss the point itself, I had still made a hundred yards or so of easting. I was, in truth, close in. I could see the cool green tree-tops swaying together in the breeze, and felt sure I'd fetch the next headland without fail.

It was high time, for I now began to be tortured by thirst. The blaze of the sun overhead, its thousandfold glare off the waves, the sea-water that splashed me and dried caking my very lips with salt — all together set my throat burning and my head aching. The sight of the trees so near had almost sickened me with longing, but the current soon swept me past the point; and as the next reach of sea opened out, I saw a sight that turned my thoughts clean around.

Right in front of me, not half a mile off, lay the Hispaniola under sail. I made sure, of course, I'd be taken; but I was in such distress for want of water that I scarcely knew whether to be glad or sorry — and long before I'd settled it, sheer surprise took over my mind, and I could do nothing but stare and wonder.

The Hispaniola was under her mainsail and two jibs, the lovely white canvas shining in the sun like snow or silver. When I first sighted her all her sails were drawing; she lay on a course about north-west, and I supposed the men aboard were rounding the island to get back to the anchorage. Presently she began to fetch more and more to the west, so that I thought they'd spotted me and were coming about to chase. At last, though, she ran right up into the wind's eye, was taken flat aback, and hung there a while helpless, her sails shivering.
“Clumsy fools,” said I; “drunk as owls still, the lot of them.” And I pictured the dance Captain Smollett would have led them.

Meanwhile the schooner fell off and filled again on another tack, ran swiftly a minute or so, then brought up once more dead in the wind's eye. Over and over it went. To and fro, up and down, north, south, east, west, the Hispaniola sailed by swoops and dashes, each time ending as she'd begun, the canvas idly flapping. It grew plain to me that no one was at the helm. And if so — where were the men? Either dead drunk or fled, I thought; and maybe, if I could get aboard, I might hand the ship back to her captain.

The current was carrying coracle and schooner south at the same rate. As for the schooner's sailing, it was so wild and broken, and she hung so long in irons each time, that she certainly gained nothing — perhaps even lost. If only I dared sit up and paddle, I felt sure I could run her down. The scheme had an air of adventure that fired me, and the thought of the water-cask by the fore companion doubled my rising courage.

Up I got, and was greeted almost at once by another cloud of spray; but this time I held to my purpose and set myself, with all my strength and care, to paddle after the unsteered Hispaniola. Once I shipped so heavy a sea that I had to stop and bale, my heart fluttering like a bird's; but little by little I got the knack of it, and steered my coracle among the waves with only now and then a knock on her bows and a dash of foam in my face.

I was gaining fast on the schooner now; I could see the brass glinting on the tiller as it banged to and fro, and still not a soul showed on her decks. I couldn't but suppose her deserted. If not, the men must be lying drunk below, where I might batten them down, perhaps, and do as I pleased with the ship.

For some while she'd been doing the worst thing possible for me — standing still. She headed nearly due south, yawing, of course, all the time. Each time she fell off, her sails part-filled and brought her in a moment right up to the wind again. The worst thing possible, I say, for helpless as she looked, with the canvas cracking like guns and the blocks rattling and banging about the deck, she still kept running from me — not only with the speed of the current but by the whole of her leeway, which was naturally great.

But now, at last, my chance came. The breeze fell very low for a few seconds, and the current, slowly turning her, brought the Hispaniola round on her centre until she showed me her stern, the cabin window still gaping open and the lamp over the table still burning on into the day. The mainsail hung drooped like a banner. She was stock-still but for the current.
For the last little while I'd actually been losing ground; but now, redoubling my efforts, I began once more to gain on the chase.
I was within a hundred yards of her when the wind clapped down again; she filled on the port tack and went off afresh, dipping and skimming like a swallow.

My first impulse was despair, my second joy. Round she came, till she lay broadside to me — round still, till she had covered a half, then two-thirds, then three-quarters of the gap between us. I could see the water boiling white under her forefoot. Vastly tall she looked to me, down in my little coracle.

And then, all at once, I began to understand. I had scarce time to think — scarce time to act and save myself. I was on the crest of one swell as the schooner came stooping over the next. The bowsprit was right over my head. I sprang to my feet and leaped, stamping the coracle under water as I went. One hand caught the jib-boom, my foot lodged between the stay and the brace; and as I clung there panting, a dull blow told me the schooner had charged down and struck the coracle, and that I was left, with no way back, aboard the Hispaniola.
